Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Recognize the various types of phalangeal, metacarpal, and carpal fractures.
Understand the indications for nonsurgical versus surgical management of phalangeal,
metacarpal, and carpal fractures.
Identify complications that may result from surgical and nonsurgical management of various
hand fractures.
Understand the vascular supply to the scaphoid and how it influences fracture healing.
Phalangeal Fractures




NOTES

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Phalangeal fractures are the second most common type of pediatric fracture. Proximal
phalanx fractures are the most common type of phalangeal fracture.1-3
Divided into base, shaft, neck, and condylar fractures
Goal of management is to restore stability and joint congruency and restore rotation and
angular alignment to allow for early mobility
Epidemiology
Different phalangeal fractures occur in patients of various ages.4
Distal phalanx fractures peak at age 1 year.
Other phalangeal fractures peak at age 12 years.3
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
Most hand injuries occur at the physis within the zone of hypertrophy.5
Physis is present in the proximal end of the phalanx.
Most phalangeal fractures are periarticular or extra-articular.6,7
Tendons
A predictable pattern of fracture displacement exists because of the adjacent soft-tissue
anatomy.1,7
Associated Injuries
Distal phalanx fractures may be associated with soft-tissue injury to the nail bed or the
fingertip.1,5
Proximal and middle phalanx fractures may be associated with soft-tissue and tendinous
injuries with open lacerations.2
Injury Classification

Physeal fractures are described according to the Salter-Harris classification system.
Salter-Harris type II fracture at the base of the proximal phalanx is the most common type.1
Extra-octave fracture is the eponym for a Salter Harris type II fracture in the little finger
caused by forced abduction.1,3,5-7
Salter-Harris type III fracture at the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb may
represent ulnar collateral ligament avulsion injury.1,6 (Figure 1)
Neck and shaft fractures are categorized by fracture type and displacement.
Periarticular neck fractures may be missed in young children because of the cartilaginous distal
fragment.
Distal periarticular phalanx fractures typically result from a digit being slammed in a door.1,5-8

Figure 1 Oblique (A) and PA (B) radiographs of a left thumb demonstrate a displaced Salter-
Harris type III fracture of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb, which necessitated
reduction and fixation.
Middle phalanx fractures are characterized in a manner similar to that of proximal phalanx
fractures. Fracture alignment often is determined by the surrounding tendinous anatomy.
Management is similar to that for proximal phalanx fractures.1-6
Seymour fracture: displaced distal phalanx physeal fracture with associated nail bed injury
(Figure 2).
SEND FEEDBACK

Most commonly managed surgically via removal of interposed tissue (typically the germinal
matrix), irrigation and débridement, reduction across the distal interphalangeal joint, and
nail bed repair.
Antibiotic agents are recommended given the open nature of the fracture.
Widened physis observed on imaging studies suggests interposed tissue.
Complications—Nail deformity is most common; osteomyelitis, nonunion, and malunion are
rare with appropriate diagnosis and management.1,3,5,8,9
Bony mallet fracture: fracture of the epiphysis of the dorsal distal phalanx at the extensor
attachment (Figure 3)
Present with inability to maintain active extension of the DIP joint, with full passive extension
Most common treatment option is hyperextension splinting for 6 to 8 weeks unless the joint
is incongruent.1,5
Surgical management is recommended for unstable fractures involving more than 50% of the
articular surface of the distal phalanx base, those that do not reduce with full extension of
the distal interphalangeal joint, and those with volar joint subluxation.10
Tuft fractures are fractures of the distal phalanx that typically are associated with crush
injuries and nail bed lacerations, not involving the physis. These have a broad spectrum of
presentation with regard to severity of injury and affected soft-tissue structures.
A 25% subungual hematoma may indicate a nail bed laceration.
Most require irrigation and débridement with repair of associated soft-tissue injury.
Prophylactic antibiotic agents usually are administered for 3 to 5 days after repair.1,5,6,11
Figure 2 Images of a left ring finger with a Seymour fracture. Lateral (A) and dorsal (B) view
clinical photographs show an avulsion of the proximal nail plate from the germinal matrix. PA (C)

and lateral (D) radiographs demonstrate an associated open Salter-Harris type II distal phalanx
fracture.
Figure 3 Lateral radiograph of a finger demonstrates a displaced bony mallet fracture, which is
more common in children and adolescents than a soft-tissue mallet injury because the physis is
weaker than the attachment of the terminal tendon to the epiphysis. (Courtesy of Erin M. Meisel,
MD, Los Angeles, CA.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Injury history may be limited depending on the age of the child and whether the injury was
witnessed. Mechanisms of injury vary based on fracture type.
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
6/25


Physical Examination
Physical examination of a finger injury in the pediatric population may be a challenge
depending on patient age, development, and temperament. Emergency department
anesthesia or sedation may aid in examination of painful injuries. Overlap of the digits
must be assessed on active flexion or during tenodesis under sedation to appreciate
rotational deformity (Figure 4). In addition, careful examination of nail plate orientation
may aid in assessment of rotation through a fracture.3,7
Figure 4 Clinical photographs of the hand of a 10-year-old girl with subtle malangulation
of a left little finger Salter-Harris type II proximal phalanx fracture. The deformity is not
clinically apparent dorsally (A) or palmarly (B) with the hand in extension but is observed
with the fingers in flexion (C).
Imaging Studies
Radiography

Radiography
Standard radiographic imaging studies should include PA, lateral, and oblique
views of the affected digit. A true lateral view is important for assessing the
alignment of periarticular phalangeal neck fractures and aids in decision
making. The double-density sign is critical in evaluating condylar fracture
displacement.1,3,5-7,11(Figure 5)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
7/25

Figure 5 Lateral radiograph of a finger demonstrates a middle phalanx fracture
with a double-density sign, indicative of rotational malalignment. The condyles
of the uninjured proximal phalanx are almost perfectly superimposed.
(Courtesy of Erin M. Meisel, MD, Los Angeles, CA.)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management via closed reduction and cast immobilization is appropriate for most
phalangeal fractures, with healing occurring in approximately 3 weeks8
Central slip avulsion injuries are managed similar to those in adults via splinting of the
proximal interphalangeal joint in full extension for 6 weeks, with range of motion of the distal
interphalangeal joint as tolerated.
Volar plate avulsion injuries are managed similar to those in adults via buddy taping to the
adjacent digit and early mobilization to prevent stiffness.12
Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
8/25

Less than 10° of angulation in the coronal plane because poor remodeling potential exists in
the coronal plane
No rotational deformity of the digit
Sagittal alignment has the potential to remodel if more than 2 years of growth is remaining.1,7
Techniques/Procedures

Techniques/Procedures
Stable phalanx fractures may be managed via buddy taping to adjacent digit(s). Unstable
injuries should be protected via splint or cast immobilization in the intrinsic plus
position. Management should consider the age and temperament of the child.1,5,7
Displaced Salter-Harris type II fractures may require closed reduction and splinting for
substantial angulation (Figure 6). Reduction of extra-octave fractures can be
accomplished via insertion of a pencil in the fourth web space to act as a lever to
reduction.1,3,5-7
Nondisplaced thumb ulnar collateral ligament avulsion Salter-Harris type III fractures
may be managed nonsurgically if congruent and stable. These represent the equivalent
of an adult skier’s thumb injury. Similar to adults, the presence of a Stener lesion must
be considered because it requires surgical management.1,6
Figure 6 PA (A), oblique (B), and lateral (C) radiographs of a right hand demonstrating a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
9/25

minimally displaced Salter-Harris type II fracture of the long finger proximal phalanx. D,
Clinical photograph shows scissoring, which necessitates closed reduction, buddy taping
of the index and long fingers, and cast immobilization to achieve and maintain
alignment.
Surgical Management
Indications
Most intra-articular phalangeal fractures
Displaced phalangeal neck fractures, malaligned phalangeal shaft fractures, or Salter-
Harris fractures in which closed reduction alone fails (Figure 7)
Rotation of digits causing overlap on flexion
Phalangeal angulation greater than 10° in coronal alignment in a skeletally immature
child
Displaced, unstable thumb ulnar collateral ligament avulsion Salter-Harris type III
fractures1,2,6-8,11
Displaced Seymour fractures with nail bed laceration2,3,5-9
Figure 7 PA (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of a skeletally immature patient with a
displaced phalangeal neck fracture. Dorsal displacement and clinical deformity are
observed. This type of injury is inherently unstable and necessitates closed reduction
and pin fixation to attain and maintain anatomic alignment. C, Lateral fluoroscopic image
shows anatomic reduction via pin fixation. D, Lateral radiograph obtained 2 months
postoperatively.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
10/25

Techniques/Procedures
Closed reduction and pinning is indicated for most minimally displaced intra-articular
fractures because of inherent instability of the fracture (Figure 8).
Open reduction is more likely to be necessary in patients with a condylar fracture who
present more than 4 weeks postinjury.
Open reduction increases the risk of osteonecrosis.13
Seymour fractures require irrigation and débridement with repair of the germinal
matrix and pinning if unstable after nail bed repair1,3,5,8,9 (Figure 9)
Figure 8 PA (A), oblique (B), and lateral (C) radiographs of the right small finger in a
skeletally immature patient which demonstrates a displaced unicondylar proximal
phalanx fracture. A double density sign and considerable displacement are observed on
the lateral radiograph. PA fluoroscopic images show percutaneous reduction with the
use of a towel clip (D), which allowed for closed reduction and percutaneous pinning
with the use of divergent Kirschner wires (E).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
11/25

Figure 9 Images of the left ring finger with a Seymour fracture shown in Figure 2. A,
Lateral radiograph obtained after nail plate removal, gentle irrigation and débridement,
reduction of the distal phalangeal metaphysis under the germinal matrix, repair of the
germinal matrix with the use of absorbable suture, trimming with replacement of the
nail plate into the eponychial fold to act as a stent, and the application of an external
splint. Intravenous antibiotic agents were administered in the emergency department
for the open fracture, and the patient was discharged home with oral antibiotics. B and
C, Lateral fluoroscopic images show the fracture was stable after management. D,
Lateral radiograph at 4 weeks post injury demonstrates union with no deformity and no
infection.
Complications
5% complication rate of fixation loss, infection, growth disturbance, and malunion, all
of which are relatively uncommon.2,8
Approximately 30% of patients experience postoperative stiffness, which usually
resolves with physical therapy.2
Higher risk of osteonecrosis of the phalangeal head with open reduction1,3,5,7,13
Patients with a phalangeal neck fracture managed via open reduction are more likely
to have postoperative reduced range of motion, malpositioning, and
osteonecrosis.3,5,7
Metacarpal Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
12/25

Overview
Metacarpal fractures present as various fracture patterns. They typically are divided into head,
neck, shaft, and base fractures.
Often articular or periarticular in children
Managed in a manner similar to that of adult metacarpal fractures1,6,7
Epidemiology
Metacarpal fractures often result from fights1,6,7,11
A careful physical examination should be performed to evaluate for wounds given that these
fractures may be associated with clenched fist injuries and fight bites.
Thumb metacarpal base fractures represent the most common thumb fracture6,7,

Epidemiology
The most common metacarpal fractures involve the neck and shaft. Metacarpal head
fractures are rare in children and mainly affect older pediatric patients. These are mostly
Salter-Harris type II injuries, and the fifth metacarpal is most involved.1
Anatomy and Biomechanics

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Pediatric metacarpals have thick periosteum that helps to provide stability in incomplete
fractures. The periosteum also can act as a hinge to lever the fracture fragment during
reduction. In addition, the intermetacarpal ligaments between the metacarpal heads
provide resistance to displacement in patients with a low-energy fracture. The typical
apex dorsal angulation, observed in neck and shaft fractures results from the volar pull
of the interosseous musculature.5 The physis is at the neck of all the metacarpals except
for the first metacarpal, at which it is at the base.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
13/25

Injury Classification
For physeal injuries, the Salter-Harris classification system is used.
For non-physeal fractures, classification is based on fracture location, configuration,
angulation, and displacement, similar to that for adults.
Some of these fractures are open injuries (fight bites or clenched-fist injuries)
Lacerations over the metacarpophalangeal joints should be evaluated to rule out such an
injury.8
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Physical Examination
Assess the overall alignment of the digit.
Evaluate the amount of rotation or overlap on flexion of the digits; accept less than 5° of
rotation.
Essential to evaluate for a wound from mouth contact during fighting7,8,11
Imaging Studies
Radiography
PA, lateral, and oblique radiographs of the hand
Oblique view can amplify the amount of fracture angulation
Obtain a lateral view to determine angulation
Metacarpal shortening of as much as 1 cm may lead to 50% decreased grip strength.7
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Metacarpal neck and shaft fractures are most often managed nonsurgically. Apex dorsal
angulation can be reduced via the Jahss maneuver.
Dorsally directed force to a 90° flexed proximal phalanx
Counter pressure directed palmarly at the fracture site
Splint/cast immobilization in intrinsic plus position
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
14/25

Excessive angulation may lead to a dorsal prominence at the fracture site and loss of the
native appearing contour at the metacarpophalangeal joint dorsally1,6,7

Nonsurgical Management
Rotational malalignment is not acceptable because it will not remodel. Acceptable
sagittal angulation increases from radial to ulnar, similar to that in adults. Nonsurgical
treatment recommendations for the second and third metacarpals is less than 10° to 20°
of flexion in the neck and less than 10° of flexion in the shaft. Fourth and fifth
metacarpal angulation recommendations are less than 30° to 60° in the neck and 20° in
the shaft. However, these recommendations vary in the literature. Remodeling potential
in children is greater than that in the adult population; therefore, more displacement can
be accepted1,7,8,11
Diaphyseal and metaphyseal thumb metacarpal fractures also can be successfully
managed via closed reduction and immobilization
30° of angulation is acceptable
Thumb spica splint/cast after closed reduction1,8,11
Salter Harris type II and type IV thumb metacarpal fractures may have radial or ulnar
metaphyseal fragments. Radially angulated fractures usually are stable, whereas ulnarly
angulated fractures often are unstable because of the pull of the adductor pollicis brevis
and first extensor compartment; therefore, they often necessitate surgical management
for stabilization1,7 (Figure 10).

15/25

Figure 10 PA (A), oblique (B), and lateral (C) radiographs of a right hand which
demonstrate a Salter-Harris type II fracture of the right thumb metacarpal with ulnar
displacement. This type of injury is inherently unstable because of the multiple strong
muscular forces on the first ray. PA (D) and lateral (E) fluoroscopic images demonstrate
reduction and pinning for stabilization.
Surgical Management
Salter Harris type III/IV fractures
Represent Bennett fracture equivalent6-8,11

Surgical Management
Substantially displaced metacarpal neck and shaft fractures can be managed via closed
reduction and percutaneous pinning with the use of Kirschner wires. Open reduction
and internal fixation may be required if closed reduction is unsuccessful.
Intra-articular physeal fractures of the base of the thumb metacarpal often require
surgical management because of instability and/or intra-articular step-off.
Indications
Metacarpal neck and shaft fractures

16/25

Excessive angulation
Rotational malalignment
Fight bite open injuries7,8
Complications
Metacarpal head fractures
Associated with osteonecrosis and growth arrest
Likely because of intracapsular hematoma
May be reduced with hematoma aspiration at the time of reduction
Limit multiple attempts at reduction1,6,7
Metacarpal neck and shaft fractures
Adhesions to overlying extensor tendons
Important to start early digit range of motion7
Thumb metacarpal base Salter-Harris type III fractures
Although rare, poor reduction may lead to posttraumatic degenerative arthritis.6
Malalignment

Malalignment
The most common complication is malalignment. This includes rotational deformity,
which results in overlapping digits on flexion. Correction of malalignment requires late
osteotomy.7,8
Carpal Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Epidemiology
Scaphoid fractures are the most common carpal bone fracture in children.
Incidence peaks at age 15 years5
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
17/25

71% of scaphoid fractures are waist fractures.
23% of scaphoid fractures occur at distal pole.
6% of scaphoid fractures are located at the proximal pole.1,2,14
As participation in youth and extreme sports increases, the incidence of scaphoid fractures
also increases15

Epidemiology
Scaphoid fractures only represent 3% of pediatric hand and wrist fractures; however,
they are the most common carpal bone fracture in children. Because the ossific nucleus
of the scaphoid is not visible radiographically until patients are aged 4 to 5 years,
scaphoid fractures rarely are diagnosed in patients younger than 6 years. These are
described as proximal pole, waist, or distal pole fractures, depending upon the location
of the fracture.5,16 Capitate fractures are the second most common pediatric carpal
bone fracture. These usually are minimally displaced but may be associated with other
carpal bone injuries.16
Hook of hamate fractures represent 2% of all carpal bone fractures.
Other carpal bone fractures, including the lunate, triquetrum, trapezoid, and pisiform,
are rare.16
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Diagnosis and management of pediatric carpal bone fractures must consider the bone
ossification and blood supply.
Osteology
Ossific nucleus in the scaphoid appears at age 4 to 5 years
Scaphoid finishes ossification at age 13 to 15 years5,16
Vascular Anatomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
18/25

Blood supply enters the scaphoid dorsally and traverses in a retrograde fashion
Ossification follows the blood supply pattern distal to proximal5
Capitate also has retrograde blood supply16
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Scaphoid fractures usually result from a fall onto an outstretched hand.8,17 The
incidence of scaphoid fractures appears to be increasing because of high body mass
index and higher energy sporting activities in the pediatric population.2,3,14,15
Hook of hamate fractures typically occur during sporting activities that require gripping a
club, racquet, or bat. Fracture also may result from a fall onto an outstretched hand,
landing on the ulnar border, or attempting to catch a hard ball.16,17
Associated Injuries
Dorsal intercalated segment instability deformity from scaphoid nonunion in children does not
progress to scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse of the wrist, dissimilar from that in the adult
population.
Dorsal intercalated segment instability deformity may persist even after successful surgical
management of nonunion with bone grafting.1,5,14
Injury Classification
Scaphoid fractures are anatomically described as proximal pole, waist, or distal pole fractures.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Because 13% to 30% of scaphoid fractures are missed on initial radiographs, a thorough
physical examination is crucial.5,6
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
19/25

Physical Examination
Scaphoid fracture
Volar scaphoid tenderness, pain with radial deviation, pain with active range of motion of the
wrist
Anatomic snuffbox tenderness1,3
Hook of hamate fracture
Vague pain at the volar ulnar hand and forearm during gripping
Callus or skin changes over the volar hamate
Decreased grip strength
Tenderness at the hook of hamate16,17
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Scaphoid fracture
AP wrist, lateral, and scaphoid views• Fractures rarely are diagnosed before age 6 years
because the scaphoid is mostly cartilage.
13% to 37% of patients with a scaphoid fracture have initial radiographs that are negative.
Repeat radiographs 10 to 14 days after initial injury.1-3,16
Hook of hamate fracture
Not visualized on conventional wrist radiographs
Can be visualized on carpal tunnel view
CT consistently demonstrates fracture16,17
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Helpful to rule out occult scaphoid fracture shortly after injury
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Slower time to union and increased nonunion rates have been noted in chronic fractures,
displaced fractures, and proximal pole fractures.1,2,8,14
Chronic scaphoid fractures heal 23% of the time via cast immobilization alone.1,5,17
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
20/25

Displaced waist fractures and proximal pole fractures managed nonsurgically are associated
with a healing rate of less than 50%1,17
Distal pole fractures managed in a closed fashion routinely heal within 4 to 8 weeks.5,17
Waist fractures may take 5 to 16 weeks before radiographic healing is observed.5,17
Waist fractures are associated with poorer results (especially in adolescents) and may result in
osteonecrosis and/or nonunion.2,3,8
Clinical suspicion should guide management; the standard of care is to immobilize all
suspected scaphoid fractures and obtain repeat radiographs in 10 to 14 days.6,11,16
Scaphoid fractures are most commonly managed via a short arm or long arm thumb spica
cast.
Nondisplaced hook of hamate fractures may heal with a period of short arm cast
immobilization.17 Hook of hamate fracture nonunions do not routinely heal with
immobilization alone.16
Nondisplaced capitate fractures generally heal with cast immobilization. Displaced fractures
may require prompt open reduction and internal fixation to prevent osteonecrosis of the
proximal pole.16
Surgical Management

Surgical Management
Displaced scaphoid waist fractures should be managed via open reduction and internal
fixation (Figure 11). In patients with an identified scaphoid nonunion, treatment requires
open reduction, internal fixation, and possibly bone grafting. Nonunion may result from
late presentation and diagnosis, improper immobilization, or late fracture displacement.
Surgical fixation for nonunions in pediatric patients has commonly involved a volar
approach with autologous bone grafting and fixation with the use of Kirschner wires or
permanent screws, similar to treatment in adults. More recent literature has found that
narrow diameter headless screw fixation shortens the time to healing in older
adolescents.1,5,14 Gholson et al14 reported an increased time to union in patients with
open physes, considerably displaced fractures, proximal pole fractures, certain
compression screw types, and use of bone graft.1,2,8
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Phalangeal, Metacarpal and Carpal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000525
21/25

Hook of hamate fracture management often requires excision of the bony fragment.17
Capitate nonunion is rare but requires bone grafting and internal fixation.16
Figure 11 Radiographs of the wrist of a 12-year-old girl who fell onto her wrist. PA (A)
and scaphoid (B) radiographs obtained 4 weeks postinjury demonstrate a displaced
scaphoid waist fracture. PA (C) and scaphoid (D) radiographs obtained 3 months after
open reduction and internal fixation with the use of a headless compression screw via a
dorsal approach demonstrate fracture union.
Complications
Scaphoid proximal pole and waist fractures: chronic pain and disability, osteonecrosis, and
nonunion.1,2,8
Hook of hamate fracture nonunion may lead to persistent pain and rare tendon rupture.16,17
Mark as Complete
